questions.question: A palmitate molecule in the cytosol will be oxidized in the mitochondrial matrix. In what order does it meet these enzymes and transporters on the way in?
options: CAT1 → acyl-CoA synthetase → acylcarnitine translocase → CAT2
Acyl-CoA synthetase → acylcarnitine translocase → CAT1 → CAT2
Acyl-CoA synthetase → CAT1 → acylcarnitine translocase → CAT2
Acylcarnitine translocase → acyl-CoA synthetase → CAT2 → CAT1
Acyl-CoA synthetase → CAT2 → acylcarnitine translocase → CAT1
questions.explanation: Acyl-CoA synthetase first activates the fatty acid in the cytosol, using ATP. CAT1 on the outer membrane moves the acyl group from CoA to carnitine. The translocase carries acylcarnitine across the inner membrane, and CAT2 moves the acyl group back onto matrix CoA for β-oxidation. Trap: B puts transport before CAT1. The translocase carries acylcarnitine, not acyl-CoA, so CAT1 has to act first.

questions.question: Compare one β-oxidation turn of equal-length saturated acyl-CoA and a substrate already containing a trans-Δ² double bond. Downstream enzymes work normally. Which products differ for the trans-Δ² substrate?
options: The same acetyl-CoA and NADH, but one fewer FADH₂.
The same acetyl-CoA and FADH₂, but one fewer NADH.
One fewer acetyl-CoA, with unchanged NADH and FADH₂.
The same acetyl-CoA, but one fewer NADH and one fewer FADH₂.
The same acetyl-CoA, NADH, and FADH₂.
questions.explanation: The existing trans-Δ² bond lets the substrate enter at hydration. It bypasses the first oxidation and its FAD reduction. Hydration, NAD⁺-dependent hydroxyl oxidation, and thiolysis can still occur, so that turn retains its NADH and acetyl-CoA production. Trap: D treats both oxidations as redundant. The pre-existing double bond replaces the first oxidation, not the later hydroxyl-to-ketone oxidation.

questions.question: An acetyl-CoA carboxylase variant makes carboxybiotin, and its isolated transfer site works. Yet its biotin arm cannot reach that site in the intact enzyme. ATP is consumed but little malonyl-CoA forms. Which interpretation fits?
options: Bicarbonate activation is defective; adding NADPH should restore it.
The transfer site has lost acetyl-CoA specificity despite its normal separate assay.
ATP consumption demonstrates that the complete carboxylation cycle is functioning.
The arm normally transfers ATP between sites; carboxybiotin can diffuse independently.
Activation can occur without productive delivery of the activated carbon to acetyl-CoA.
questions.explanation: The two chemical sites must communicate through the attached biotin carrier. Successful activation and a competent transfer site do not establish successful overall turnover when the carrier cannot reach the second site. ATP use by the first stage is therefore insufficient evidence of malonyl-CoA synthesis. Trap: C confuses energy consumption with productive coupling. The product must be measured as well as ATP use.

An eight-carbon chain retaining no labels; six NADPH consumed.
An eleven-carbon chain retaining three labels; six NADPH consumed.
An eight-carbon chain retaining no labels; three NADPH consumed.
A six-carbon chain retaining no labels; six NADPH consumed.
questions.explanation: Each malonyl donor contributes two retained carbons; its extra carboxyl carbon leaves as CO₂ during condensation. The starter plus three additions therefore contains eight carbons and none of these labels. Keto reduction and enoyl reduction each consume NADPH, giving six NADPH over three cycles. Trap: A retains the temporary carboxyl labels, but those specific carbons leave as CO₂ during condensation.

questions.question: For the glucose ring shown, which carbon is the anomeric carbon, and which is the penultimate (configurational) carbon that makes it a D-sugar?
options: C5 is anomeric; C1 is penultimate.
C1 is anomeric; C1 is also penultimate.
C2 is anomeric; C5 is penultimate.
C1 is anomeric; C5 is penultimate.
C1 is anomeric; C6 is penultimate.
questions.explanation: The anomeric carbon is the former carbonyl carbon: C1 in an aldose like glucose. It is the ring carbon bonded to two oxygens. The penultimate carbon is the last chiral carbon, C5 in a hexose; its configuration (CH₂OH up in a D-Haworth ring, OH on the right in Fischer) makes the sugar D. Trap: E picks C6, the last carbon. C6 is not chiral, so the configurational carbon is the one before it.

questions.question: In the Fischer projection, hydroxyl I or II attacks C2 to close a ring. Which ring sizes result, and does either closure invert the original C5 configuration? Count the ring oxygen.
options: I makes a six-membered ring; II a five-membered ring; C5 is unchanged.
I makes a five-membered ring; II a six-membered ring; C5 is unchanged.
I makes a five-membered ring; II a six-membered ring; C5 is inverted in II.
Both make six-membered rings; C5 is unchanged.
Both make five-membered rings; C5 is inverted in I.
questions.explanation: Route I encloses O5 and C2–C5, five atoms. Route II encloses O6 and C2–C6, six atoms. Both closures create an anomeric center at the former carbonyl carbon without inverting the pre-existing C5 stereocenter or changing the six-carbon skeleton. Trap: A reverses the two ring sizes. Include the attacking oxygen and trace the enclosed carbon chain when counting atoms.

questions.question: Only three of the ten glycolytic enzymes are major control points. Which three, and why those?
options: Aldolase, triose phosphate isomerase, and GAPDH, because they split and oxidize the sugar.
Hexokinase, PFK-1, and pyruvate kinase, because all three make ATP.
Hexokinase, aldolase, and pyruvate kinase, because they have the largest positive ΔG′°.
PFK-1, GAPDH, and phosphoglycerate kinase, because they use or make ATP or NADH.
Hexokinase, PFK-1, and pyruvate kinase, because their ΔG in the cell is large and negative.
questions.explanation: Hexokinase, PFK-1, and pyruvate kinase have large negative ΔG values in the cell, so they run essentially one way and set the pathway’s flux. The other seven steps run near equilibrium (ΔG ≈ 0) and follow concentrations, so regulating them would not control flux. Trap: B names the right enzymes for the wrong reason: hexokinase and PFK-1 consume ATP rather than make it.

questions.question: Aldolase cleavage has a positive standard free-energy change but proceeds in cells. DHAP rises twentyfold while GAP, F1,6BP, temperature, and enzyme amount stay fixed. What happens to the driving force for cleavage?
options: It becomes more favorable because product accumulation lowers the reaction quotient.
It is unchanged because the standard free-energy change has not changed.
It becomes more favorable because extra DHAP is an additional cleavage substrate.
It becomes less favorable because the product-to-reactant quotient increases.
It becomes less favorable because DHAP changes the equilibrium constant at fixed temperature.
questions.explanation: Cellular free energy depends on concentrations as well as the standard value. Raising a cleavage product increases the reaction quotient and shifts the driving force against further cleavage. Product removal can support forward flux; product accumulation opposes that contribution without changing the equilibrium constant. Trap: B notices that the standard value stays fixed but omits the concentration-dependent term in cellular free energy.

questions.question: Arsenate bypasses ATP formation at phosphoglycerate kinase for both GAP molecules from each glucose. Other glycolytic steps work, and all pyruvate becomes lactate. What are the net ATP and NADH gains per glucose? (Think about what happens to the NADH when pyruvate becomes lactate.)
options: Zero ATP and zero NADH.
Two ATP and zero NADH.
Zero ATP and two NADH.
Two ATP and two NADH.
Negative two ATP and zero NADH.
questions.explanation: Two ATP are invested. Bypassing phosphoglycerate kinase loses its two ATP, while the two pyruvate kinase reactions still make two ATP, leaving zero net ATP. GAPDH still forms two NADH, which are consumed when two pyruvate are reduced to lactate, leaving no net NADH gain. Trap: C counts NADH formation at GAPDH but stops the accounting before lactate dehydrogenase consumes it.

questions.question: Phosphoglycerate kinase makes ATP in glycolysis, yet gluconeogenesis runs the same enzyme in reverse. Why can it run both ways?
options: In the cell it only runs toward 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate; the ATP is made elsewhere.
Its ΔG′° is close to zero, so both directions are equally favorable.
Its ΔG′° is negative, but cellular concentrations keep its actual ΔG near zero, so the direction follows the concentrations.
Phosphorylation during fasting reverses its direction.
ATP binding at an allosteric site reverses the enzyme.
questions.explanation: ΔG′° (about −18.5 kJ/mol) describes standard conditions. In the cell, the ratio of products to reactants keeps the actual ΔG near zero, so the direction follows concentrations. That is why gluconeogenesis can run this ATP-making step backward. Pyruvate kinase is the payoff step whose cellular ΔG stays large and negative. Trap: B confuses ΔG′° with ΔG. The standard value is not near zero; the cellular value is.

questions.question: Test [1-¹³C]G6P and [6-¹³C]G6P in separate systems: one performs only oxidative PPP; the other only glycolysis to pyruvate. Exclude carbon recycling and pyruvate oxidation. Which initial labeling pattern distinguishes them? (Draw it out.)
options: Both labels immediately yield ¹³CO₂ in the oxidative PPP; neither is retained in pentose.
Only the C6 label yields ¹³CO₂ in the oxidative PPP; glycolysis releases the C1 label.
The C1 label yields ¹³CO₂ in both pathways because glucose oxidation always removes C1.
The oxidative PPP releases the C1 label but retains C6 in pentose; glycolysis releases neither as CO₂.
Neither pathway releases either label as CO₂ until pyruvate enters mitochondria.
questions.explanation: The oxidative PPP removes glucose-6-phosphate C1 during oxidative decarboxylation; the remaining five carbons include its original C6. Glycolysis splits and rearranges the six-carbon skeleton into two three-carbon pyruvate molecules without decarboxylation. Oxidation and carbon loss are related in some reactions but are not synonymous. Trap: C assumes all oxidation must release CO₂, overlooking carbon conservation during glycolysis.

questions.question: Ten glucose units enter an anaerobic muscle extract as G1P released by glycogen phosphorylase. All ten become lactate through glycolysis. What is the net ATP yield from G1P to lactate?
options: 20 ATP.
30 ATP.
40 ATP.
10 ATP.
Zero ATP.
questions.explanation: G1P becomes G6P without using ATP, so this starting point bypasses hexokinase’s investment. PFK-1 uses one ATP per glucose unit, while phosphoglycerate kinase and pyruvate kinase produce four in total. The net is three ATP per G1P, or thirty for ten units. Lactate formation regenerates NAD⁺ without adding ATP. Trap: A applies the two-ATP net yield for free glucose, incorrectly charging these G1P inputs for a hexokinase step they bypass.

questions.question: A gluconeogenic extract receives two PEP instead of two pyruvate. All later enzymes work; no other pathway regenerates ATP or NADH. Which nucleotide and reducing-cofactor inputs remain necessary to make one glucose?
options: Four ATP, two GTP, and two NADH.
Two ATP and two GTP, but no NADH.
Two ATP and two NADH, but no GTP.
Two NADH, but no ATP or GTP.
Two ATP, but no GTP or NADH.
questions.explanation: Supplying PEP bypasses the two pyruvate carboxylase reactions and the two PEPCK reactions, avoiding two ATP and two GTP. Reverse phosphoglycerate kinase still consumes two ATP, and reverse GAPDH still consumes two NADH. The phosphatase bypasses do not turn those hydrolyses into ATP production. Trap: D correctly removes the pyruvate-to-PEP costs but forgets ATP consumption at reverse phosphoglycerate kinase.

questions.question: Liver glucokinase (hexokinase IV) differs from muscle hexokinase I. Which pair of properties lets the liver phosphorylate glucose in proportion to blood glucose?
options: Low Km and strong inhibition by G6P, so it works at all glucose levels.
High Km and strong inhibition by G6P, so it stops once G6P forms.
Low Km, so it traps glucose even when blood glucose is low.
The same Km as hexokinase I, but more enzyme is present.
High Km and no inhibition by G6P, so its rate tracks blood glucose and it keeps working after a meal.
questions.explanation: Glucokinase’s high Km means its rate rises and falls with blood glucose over the normal range. Because G6P does not inhibit it, the liver keeps capturing glucose after a meal. Hexokinase I has a low Km, is nearly saturated at normal glucose, and shuts off as G6P builds. Trap: C: a low Km would trap glucose even when the liver should be releasing it during fasting.

questions.question: The plot compares normal PFK-1 with a variant. F6P, free Mg²⁺, pH, and enzyme amount are fixed. Which ATP-binding change best explains the variant?
options: Weaker ATP binding at the inhibitory regulatory site, with catalytic ATP use largely retained.
Loss of catalytic ATP binding, with inhibitory ATP binding unchanged.
Stronger ATP binding only at the catalytic site, with inhibitory ATP binding unchanged.
Stronger inhibitory ATP binding, causing the normal high-ATP decrease to disappear.
Removal of all ATP binding, allowing F6P alone to form fructose-1,6-bisphosphate.
questions.explanation: ATP first supports catalysis as a substrate. At higher concentrations it also inhibits through a separate regulatory site. Preserved low-ATP rates plus loss of high-ATP suppression fit weakened inhibitory binding while the catalytic ATP site continues to function. Trap: B would impair the low-ATP reactions that still behave normally; it also leaves the inhibitory effect in place.

questions.question: Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate rises in the fed liver. What does it do, and why is one regulator acting on two enzymes useful?
options: It inhibits PFK-1 and activates FBPase-1, so the fed liver makes glucose.
It activates both PFK-1 and FBPase-1, so both pathways speed up together.
It activates PFK-1 and inhibits FBPase-1, so one signal turns glycolysis on and gluconeogenesis off at the same step.
It is a glycolytic intermediate that aldolase splits into two trioses.
It activates PFK-1 only; FBPase-1 is controlled only by insulin.
questions.explanation: F2,6BP activates PFK-1 and inhibits FBPase-1. Raising it turns glycolysis on and gluconeogenesis off at the same F6P/F1,6BP step, so the liver never runs both directions at once. Trap: A reverses the effects. That is what low F2,6BP does during fasting.

questions.question: GSK3 phosphorylates and inactivates glycogen synthase. Insulin inactivates GSK3. What is the net effect of insulin on glycogen synthase?
options: Synthase becomes more phosphorylated and less active.
No effect, because GSK3 regulates only glycogen phosphorylase.
Synthase becomes less phosphorylated and less active.
Synthase becomes less phosphorylated and more active, so glucose is stored.
Synthase becomes more phosphorylated and more active.
questions.explanation: GSK3 phosphorylates and inactivates glycogen synthase. Insulin inactivates GSK3 (and activates PP1), so synthase ends up less phosphorylated and more active, and the fed liver stores glucose. Inhibiting an inhibitor activates the target. Trap: A applies “insulin means phosphorylation.” Here insulin blocks the kinase, so phosphorylation falls.

questions.question: Liver and muscle lose glycogen and form G6P at similar rates. Only liver releases much free glucose; muscle produces more glycolytic products. Which conclusion fits?
options: Comparable mobilization can support different outputs because muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase and uses G6P locally.
The muscle phosphorylase must be inactive because little free glucose appears.
Liver phosphorylase releases free glucose directly, whereas muscle phosphorylase releases G1P.
Muscle lacks phosphoglucomutase, even though G6P formation was measured.
The liver’s glucose release demonstrates that it is simultaneously activating glycogen synthase.
questions.explanation: Glycogen disappearance and G6P formation establish mobilization in both preparations. Glucose-6-phosphatase permits liver to generate free glucose for release. Skeletal muscle lacks that terminal activity and can use the phosphorylated carbon in glycolysis. Free glucose output alone is therefore an inadequate assay of muscle glycogen breakdown. Trap: B equates absence of an exported end product with absence of upstream pathway flux.

questions.question: Phosphoglucomutase converts G1P to G6P using a phosphorylated serine. What role does the serine’s phosphate play?
options: It is an insulin signal that switches the enzyme on.
It is hydrolyzed to supply energy for the reaction.
It binds ATP, which donates the phosphate to C6.
It is released as free Pi at the end of each reaction.
It is handed to the sugar to make glucose-1,6-bisphosphate; the enzyme then takes back the C1 phosphate, re-phosphorylating the serine.
questions.explanation: The phosphoserine donates its phosphate to C6 of G1P, forming glucose-1,6-bisphosphate. The enzyme then takes back the C1 phosphate, leaving G6P and a re-phosphorylated serine. If the serine started unphosphorylated, the product would not be released. Trap: A treats this as a regulatory phosphorylation. This phosphate is part of the catalytic cycle.

questions.question: After a carbohydrate-rich meal, malonyl-CoA rises in the liver. Why does this slow β-oxidation?
options: Malonyl-CoA is oxidized in place of fatty acids.
Malonyl-CoA inhibits CAT1, so fatty acids can’t enter the mitochondria to be oxidized while new ones are being made.
Malonyl-CoA directly inhibits acyl-CoA dehydrogenase in the matrix.
Malonyl-CoA uses up the cell’s CoA.
Malonyl-CoA activates fatty acid synthase, which shares its enzymes with β-oxidation.
questions.explanation: Malonyl-CoA, made by acetyl-CoA carboxylase in the committed step of fatty acid synthesis, inhibits CAT1. Newly made fatty acids therefore aren’t sent into the mitochondria to be burned, preventing a futile cycle. Trap: E: synthesis and β-oxidation use different enzymes in different compartments. The link between them is the malonyl-CoA signal.

questions.question: Glycogen phosphorylase breaks glycosidic bonds with Pi instead of water. What is the advantage?
options: The glucose leaves already phosphorylated, saving the ATP hexokinase would spend and keeping the sugar trapped in the cell.
Phosphorolysis releases free glucose that can leave the cell directly.
Pi is needed to regenerate pyridoxal phosphate after each reaction.
Hydrolysis would produce G6P, which cannot enter glycolysis.
Using Pi makes the reaction irreversible.
questions.explanation: Pi attack releases G1P, which phosphoglucomutase converts to G6P without spending ATP. Glucose from glycogen therefore enters glycolysis one ATP cheaper than free glucose, and the phosphorylated sugar cannot leave the cell. Trap: B: free glucose would need hexokinase’s ATP and could leak out. The liver makes free glucose later, using glucose-6-phosphatase.

questions.question: Galactose enters glycolysis with the help of UDP-sugars. Which statement is correct?
options: Galactokinase uses UDP-glucose instead of ATP.
An epimerase converts free galactose to glucose before any phosphorylation.
Galactose-1-phosphate swaps onto UDP, releasing glucose-1-phosphate; epimerase then turns UDP-galactose back into UDP-glucose, so UDP-glucose is recycled.
Galactose enters glycolysis directly as fructose-6-phosphate.
One UDP-glucose is consumed for every galactose, so galactose costs an extra UTP.
questions.explanation: Galactokinase uses ATP to make galactose-1-phosphate. Uridylyltransferase swaps it onto UDP: Gal1P + UDP-glucose → UDP-galactose + G1P. Epimerase flips C4 to regenerate UDP-glucose. UDP-glucose works catalytically, so there is no net UTP cost. Trap: E: UDP-glucose is regenerated each turn, not consumed.

questions.question: Why does the liver regulate PFK-1 and FBPase-1 in opposite directions instead of letting both run?
options: Both enzymes compete for the same active site.
If both ran, F6P and F1,6BP would cycle with no net change while ATP is hydrolyzed every turn.
FBPase-1 would make ATP and overload the cell with energy.
Running both would use up the cell’s NAD⁺.
PFK-1 is needed only in muscle.
questions.explanation: If PFK-1 and FBPase-1 ran together, F6P → F1,6BP → F6P would cycle with no net change in sugar while each turn hydrolyzed one ATP (ATP + H₂O → ADP + Pi). Reciprocal regulation prevents this futile cycle. Trap: C: FBPase-1 releases Pi; it does not make ATP.

questions.question: Mixture I uses oxidative PPP enzymes to process one G6P with NADP⁺; II uses nonoxidative enzymes and cofactors to process two xylulose-5-phosphate and one ribose-5-phosphate. Exclude other pathways and recycling. Which net products are correct?
options: I: pentose + NADPH. II: 2 F6P + GAP + 2 NADPH.
I: pentose + 2 NADH + CO₂. II: F6P + 3 GAP.
I: 2 pentoses + CO₂. II: 2 F6P + GAP + CO₂.
I: pentose + 2 NADPH + CO₂. II: 2 F6P + GAP.
I: pentose + 2 NADPH + CO₂. II: F6P + 3 GAP, using 2 NADPH.
questions.explanation: The oxidative phase performs two NADP⁺ reductions and removes one carbon from G6P as CO₂, leaving a pentose phosphate. Nonoxidative transfer reactions conserve all fifteen supplied carbons as two six-carbon F6P plus one three-carbon GAP; they neither produce NADPH nor release CO₂ in that conversion. Trap: E conserves fifteen carbons but gives the wrong nonoxidative product ratio and incorrectly assigns a redox requirement to carbon rearrangement.

questions.question: Completely oxidize one free C14:0 fatty acid. Credit 2.5 ATP per NADH, 1.5 per FADH₂, and 10 per acetyl-CoA oxidized in the TCA cycle. Activation costs two ATP equivalents. What is the net ATP yield?
options: 94 ATP.
96 ATP.
22 ATP.
70 ATP.
92 ATP.
questions.explanation: C14:0 yields seven acetyl-CoA in six β-oxidation turns. Those turns produce six NADH and six FADH₂, worth 15 and 9 ATP. The seven acetyl-CoA contribute 70 ATP using the stated TCA credit. Subtract the two-ATP-equivalent activation cost: 15 + 9 + 70 − 2 = 92 ATP. Trap: A counts the 94 ATP produced but forgets the activation cost. B counts seven oxidative turns instead of six.
